name: Charcoal Grey
lede: Charcoal grey is the dark, slightly cool grey of burnt wood, and for a short stretch in the 1890s it was also a tube of artists' paint.

sections.title: Burnt wood, then paint
sections.body:
Paterson defines *charcoal grey* simply as a dark grey, and lists *charcoal brown* beside it as a dark brown [1]. The Pigment Compendium records a pigment sold under the name: British colourmen Winsor and Newton and Reeves supplied it in the 1890s, made from charcoal [2].

The pigment is a small footnote. Most of what the name means today comes from the material itself, charcoal, rather than from any one maker's tube.

sections.title: Where the swatch comes from
sections.body:
Four sources in our library carry the name: RAL in 1927, Maerz and Paul in 1930, ISCC-NBS in 1955 (block 266), and the later xkcd color survey of 2010 [3]. This swatch sits in the ISCC-NBS region called dark grayish blue, 6.0 CIEDE2000 units away [3]. The color is nearly neutral, with a faint cool lean, and it is close to [[dark-slate-grey]] and [[slate-grey]].

The Compendium files the pigment under the chars sub-group of the carbon-based blacks [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Dark greys of this kind are common in paint. In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color within six units of this swatch covers at least five per cent of the canvas in 1,432 works, about 6 per cent [4]. It is a shadow color in two-thirds of those pictures, and nearly never a highlight [4]. The share doubles in the twentieth century: 12.8 per cent of the 1,674 paintings dated 1900 to 1999, against 6.1 per cent in the 1800s, a lift of 2.1 over the archive as a whole [4].

In printed English the word *charcoal* peaks in 1808 and slowly falls [4]. As always these are photographs of varnished paintings, so the greys are as photographed [4].

notes.cite: Paterson, A Dictionary of Colour, pp. 96, 468

questions.q: Who sold charcoal grey as an artists' pigment in the 1890s?
True or false: in our paintings archive, this grey is rarely a shadow color.

openers: Charcoal grey was once a tube of paint: Winsor and Newton and Reeves sold it in the 1890s.
Look for this grey in the shadows: two-thirds of its appearances in our museum archive are the darkest tones.
